summary: Internal host 192.168.10.8 (win-vista, a Windows Vista workstation on the victim LAN) is very likely scanning ports across the internal network. In the alerted flow it sent 2 SYN packets with no payload to 192.168.10.17 (ubuntu-14-64) on port 61770, and the target answered with 2 RSTs. That means the port was closed, and it also shows 192.168.10.8 started the connection, so the direction is not reversed. Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 made 10,058 flows to 496 hosts on 1,060 ports. In about 29 minutes it made 503 flows to 192.168.10.17 alone, across 336 ports. All 10 neighbouring flows I scored from this pair also alert as port_scan. Neither host is a known attacker, so a scan coming from a workstation points to the source being compromised. The scan most likely ended at the closed-port stage: nothing shows a service on the target answering.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 3083227: 192.168.10.8:3031 -> 192.168.10.17:61770/TCP, duration 0.062 ms, 2 forward and 2 backward packets, 0 bytes in each direction, SYN count 2, RST count 2.
Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 made 10,058 flows to 496 distinct IPs and 1,060 distinct ports. Top ports were 53, 443, 80, 135, 139 and 445.

The pair 192.168.10.8 -> 192.168.10.17 had 503 flows (first seen 18:11:34, last seen 18:40:03) to 336 distinct destination ports, including 139, 445, 25627, 1, 61770 and 137. Total bytes were 29,340 forward and 37,320 backward.

192.168.10.8 is win-vista (Windows Vista 64-bit workstation, medium criticality, victim_lan). 192.168.10.17 is ubuntu-14-64 (Ubuntu 14.04 workstation, medium criticality, victim_lan). Neither is flagged as a known attacker.
The detector scored the anchor at attack probability 0.9999, predicted family port_scan (0.99999). The main reasons were zero backward payload, very short Fwd IAT Min and 2 backward RST flags.
All 10 sampled flows between the same pair scored above the threshold and were predicted as port_scan (probability ≥0.99986).

The SYN-forward / RST-backward pattern shows 192.168.10.8 started the connection and 192.168.10.17 refused it on a closed port. This is not a reversed-direction artifact. The pattern matches a TCP SYN/connect port scan.
A workstation that is not a known attacker is scanning hundreds of internal hosts, which suggests it has been compromised and is being used for internal discovery (lateral reconnaissance).

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) and do forensic triage to find how it was compromised: malicious downloads or documents, persistence, and the scanning tool.

Look for follow-up connections from 192.168.10.8 to ports it scanned that turned out to be open, especially SMB/NetBIOS (139, 445) on internal hosts, and check for successful sessions or lateral movement.
Review outbound traffic from 192.168.10.8 (heavy 443/53/80 use) for command-and-control activity.

uncertainties: The predict_attack output was cut off after the first few predictions. The summary still says all 10 flows were above the threshold.
Packet payloads are not available, so the scanning tool cannot be identified.
I did not check whether any scanned port on 192.168.10.17 or other hosts answered with a real service. Whether the scan found open services, and so whether it achieved anything, is unconfirmed.
